Review: Units 15–19

Units 15.1, 15.3, 15.7

Negatives with "to be"

Add not after am, is, or are to make a negative sentence. For you, we, and they, we can contract to 're not or aren't. For he, she, and it, we can contract to 's not or isn't. There is no short contraction for "am not" — we only say I'm not.

I am a farmer. I am not a doctor. You're not a doctor. You aren't a doctor. He isn't from Spain. They aren't ready.

Negative forms of to be

SubjectNegativeExample
Iam notI'm not a doctor.
You / We / They're not / aren'tYou aren't a doctor.
He / She / It's not / isn'tHe isn't a teacher.

"I am not" has no short contracted negative form — we contract to "I'm not," never "I amn't."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. (I) I am a farmer.
  2. (you) You a doctor.
  3. (he) He from Spain.
  4. (she) She's a teacher.
  5. (we) We at home.
  6. (they) They ready yet.
  7. (it) It raining today.
  8. no contraction exists for this word I am tired.

Reading practice

Marco is a new student in town. "I am not from here," he tells his classmates. "I'm from Brazil." His classmate Sofia laughs. "You aren't the only new student. Two other students started this week too." Marco looks around the room. "Is that boy our teacher?" he asks. "No, he isn't," says Sofia. "He's another new student, like you. Our teacher isn't here yet." A girl walks in. "Sorry I'm late! I'm not usually late," she says. "Don't worry," says Sofia. "You aren't late. Class hasn't started yet."

Check your understanding

1. Marco is from this town.

2. Marco is the only new student.

3. The boy in the room is not the teacher.

4. The teacher has already arrived.

5. The girl who walks in is usually late.

Units 16.1, 16.3, 16.6

Present simple negative

Use do not (don't) for I, you, we, and they. Use does not (doesn't) for he, she, and it. The main verb always stays in the base form after don't or doesn't.

He does not work inside. He works outside. I work outside. I do not work inside. She doesn't like coffee. They don't live here.

Present simple negative

SubjectNegativeExample
I / You / We / Theydo not / don't + base verbI don't work inside.
He / She / Itdoes not / doesn't + base verbHe doesn't work inside.

After doesn't, the verb goes back to its base form: "He doesn't work," not "He doesn't works."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. (I) I like spicy food.
  2. (he) He work on weekends.
  3. (they) They live in this city.
  4. (she) She drink coffee.
  5. (we) We eat meat.
  6. (it) It rain much here.
  7. the verb stays in the base form after doesn't He doesn't inside.
  8. (you) You need a ticket.

Their parents don't mind the difference. "You don't need the same schedule," their mother says.

2. Lucy works at a bakery.

3. Ben has an early class.

4. Lucy gets to sleep in.

5. Their parents are upset about the difference.

Show transcript

My roommate Jin and I are very different. I get up early, but Jin doesn't get up before ten. I eat meat, but Jin doesn't. He's a vegetarian. I don't watch TV, but he watches it every night. Units 17.1, 17.8

Simple questions

To ask a yes/no question with to be, put am, is, or are before the subject. To ask a yes/no question with another verb, use Do (I/you/we/they) or Does (he/she/it) before the subject, followed by the base verb.

Are you Canadian? Do you work in an office? Does she work in a school? Is he a doctor? Do they live nearby?

Forming a yes/no question

Question typeWord orderExample
to be questionAm/Is/Are + subjectAre you tired?
other verb, I/you/we/theyDo + subject + base verbDo you work here?
other verb, he/she/itDoes + subject + base verbDoes she work here?

After Does, the verb stays in its base form: "Does she work?" not "Does she works?"

Grammar practice: choose the right question word

  1. a to be question, (you) you Canadian?
  2. (you / work) you work in an office?
  3. (she / work) she work in a school?
  4. a to be question, (he) he a doctor?
  5. (they / live) they live nearby?
  6. (it / rain) it rain a lot here?
  7. keep the verb in base form after Does Does he tea?
  8. a to be question, (we) we late?

"Does everyone take the same lunch break?" he asks. "No, we don't. It depends on your schedule."

2. Mei works in the building every day.

3. The manager works upstairs.

4. Everyone takes the same lunch break.

5. Carlos asks no questions.

Units 18.1, 18.2

Short answers

Answer a yes/no question with a short answer: a subject pronoun plus am/is/are or do/does (and not, if negative). A short answer never repeats the whole verb phrase.

Are you a doctor? Yes, I am. Do you work in an office? No, I don't. Is she a teacher? Yes, she is. Does he like coffee? No, he doesn't.

Short answers

QuestionShort yesShort no
Are you...?Yes, I am.No, I'm not.
Do you...?Yes, I do.No, I don't.
Is she...?Yes, she is.No, she isn't.
Does he...?Yes, he does.No, he doesn't.

A short answer never repeats the main verb: we say "Yes, I do," not "Yes, I do work."

Grammar practice: complete each short answer

  1. Are you tired? (yes) Yes, I .
  2. Do you like tea? (no) No, I .
  3. Is she a nurse? (yes) Yes, she .
  4. Does he work here? (no) No, he .
  5. Are they students? (yes) Yes, they .
  6. Do we need tickets? (yes) Yes, we .
  7. Is it raining? (no) No, it .
  8. Does she like coffee? (yes) Yes, she .

Units 19.1, 19.2

Open questions with "to be"

Use a question word (What, Where, Who, When, Why, How) plus am, is, or are, plus the subject, to ask for information rather than a simple yes or no. The question word always comes first.

My name is Sarah. What is your name? Where are you from? Who is that? How old is she?

Question words

Question wordAsks aboutExample
Whata thingWhat is your name?
Wherea placeWhere are you from?
Whoa personWho is that?
Howa way or conditionHow are you?

The question word always comes first, before the form of to be.

Grammar practice: choose the right question word

  1. asking for a name is your name?
  2. asking for a place are you from?
  3. asking about a person is that woman?
  4. asking about condition are you today?
  5. asking for a reason is she upset?
  6. asking for a time is the meeting?
  7. asking about a person is your teacher?
  8. asking for a place is the nearest station?

Reading practice

On the first day of camp, the counselor asks the new campers questions. "What is your name?" she asks a tall boy. "My name is Diego," he says. "Where are you from?" she continues. "I'm from Texas." She turns to a quiet girl. "How are you today?" she asks. "I'm a little nervous," the girl says. "Who is your cabin leader?" the counselor asks another camper. "I don't know yet," he says. "That's okay," says the counselor. "When is the welcome meeting? It's in ten minutes, so let's go find out together."

Check your understanding

1. Diego is from Texas.

2. The quiet girl feels very confident.

3. The camper knows who his cabin leader is.

4. The counselor asks "When is the welcome meeting?"

5. The welcome meeting is tomorrow.

Units 19.8, 19.9

Open questions using "do" and "does"

Use a question word plus do (I/you/we/they) or does (he/she/it), plus the subject, plus the base verb, to ask for information about an action.

When do you eat lunch? When does she eat lunch? Where do you work? What does he do on weekends?

Open questions with do / does

SubjectWord orderExample
I / You / We / Theyquestion word + do + subject + base verbWhere do you live?
He / She / Itquestion word + does + subject + base verbWhere does he live?

The main verb after do or does always stays in the base form: "What does she do?" not "What does she does?"

Grammar practice: choose do or does

  1. (you / eat) When you eat lunch?
  2. (she / eat) When she eat lunch?
  3. (you / work) Where you work?
  4. (he / do on weekends) What he do on weekends?
  5. (it / rain) How often it rain here?
  6. keep the verb in base form after does What does she on weekends?
  7. (they / study) Where they study?
  8. (he / finish work) When he finish work?

Reading practice

Noor is curious about her new coworker's schedule. "Where do you live?" she asks him. "I live downtown," he says. "When do you usually arrive at the office?" she asks. "I usually arrive at eight." "What does your team do on Fridays?" Noor asks. "We usually have a short meeting," he says. "How often does the team travel?" Noor continues. "We travel about twice a year," he answers. "One more question — when do you take your lunch break?" Noor asks. "Around noon," he says, smiling. "You ask a lot of questions!"

Check your understanding

1. The coworker lives downtown.

2. He usually arrives at nine.

3. The team has a short meeting on Fridays.

4. The team travels about twice a year.

5. Noor does not ask any questions.

Units 15–19

Speaking practice

Practice speaking like in a speaking exam such as IELTS. Part 1: answer short questions about you. Part 2: prepare for one minute, then talk about a topic for one to two minutes. Part 3: act out a conversation with a partner. Try first, then open the examples.

Part 1: Interview

Answer each question in one to three sentences. Don't just say "yes" or "no" — add a reason or an extra detail.

Negatives with to be

1. Are you a morning person?

Show example answer
No, I'm not. I'm a night person. I'm not happy at seven in the morning!
Negatives with to be

2. Is your hometown big?

Show example answer
No, it isn't. It's a small town, and it isn't very busy. But it's beautiful.
Present simple negative

3. What don't you like doing at home?

Show example answer
I don't like washing the dishes, and I don't like ironing. My brother doesn't like cleaning his room.
Simple questions

4. Does your best friend live near you?

Show example answer
Yes, she does. She lives on my street, so we see each other every day.
Short answers

5. Do you drink coffee?

Show example answer
Yes, I do. I drink two cups every morning.
Open questions with to be

6. Where is your favorite place in your city?

Show example answer
My favorite place is the park near my house. It's quiet and green.
Open questions with to be

7. Who is the most important person in your life?

Show example answer
My grandmother is very important to me. She's kind and funny.
Open questions with do / does

8. What do you usually do on Sundays?

Show example answer
I usually have lunch with my family. In the afternoon, I watch a movie or read.

Part 2: Long turn

You have one minute to prepare. You can write some notes. Then talk for one to two minutes.

Describe a place you like in your town.

You should say:

  • where it is
  • what it is like (and what it isn't like)
  • what people do there

and explain why you like it.

0:00 Press a button to start
Show example answer
I want to talk about a small café near my school. It's on a quiet street, next to a bookstore. It isn't big, and it isn't expensive. It's warm and very comfortable. People don't go there to talk on the phone. They read, study, or chat with friends. The owner doesn't play loud music. He plays soft jazz. I go there every Friday after class. I don't drink coffee, so I order hot chocolate. I like this café because it's calm, and the people who work there are very friendly.

Part 3: Role-plays

Work with a partner. Student A and Student B read only their own card. Then have the conversation.

A new roommate

Student A has a room for rent. Student B wants to live there. Ask and answer yes/no questions. Use short answers.

Student A

  • Ask if B is a student.
  • Ask if B smokes.
  • Ask if B cooks.
  • Ask if B has a pet.
  • Answer B's questions.

Student B

  • Answer A's questions with short answers and add information.
  • Ask if the room is big.
  • Ask if the apartment has Wi-Fi.
  • Ask if A is quiet at night.
Useful languageAre you…?Do you…?Is the room…?Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.Yes, it does. / No, it doesn't.
Show example dialogue

A: Hi! So, are you a student?

B: Yes, I am. I study medicine.

A: Do you smoke?

B: No, I don't.

A: Do you cook?

B: Yes, I do. I cook every evening.

A: Do you have a pet?

B: No, I don't. Is the room big?

A: No, it isn't, but it's very bright.

B: Does the apartment have Wi-Fi?

A: Yes, it does. It's fast, too.

B: Great. Are you quiet at night?

A: Yes, I am. I go to bed early!

B: Perfect. I'd like the room!

At the museum information desk

Student B is a tourist. Student A works at the information desk. Use the information card.

Student A

  • Information card:
  • Open 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  • Closed on Mondays
  • Ticket: $12 (students: $8)
  • Café on the second floor
  • Gift shop next to the entrance

Student B

  • Ask when the museum opens and closes.
  • Ask which day it is closed.
  • Ask how much a ticket is.
  • Ask where the café is.
  • Ask one more question.
Useful languageWhat time does it open?When is it closed?How much is a ticket?Where is the café?Thank you for your help.
Show example dialogue

B: Excuse me. What time does the museum open?

A: It opens at nine o'clock and closes at five.

B: Is it open every day?

A: No, it isn't. It's closed on Mondays.

B: How much is a ticket?

A: It's twelve dollars. For students, it's eight dollars.

B: I'm a student! And where is the café?

A: It's on the second floor.

B: Is there a gift shop?

A: Yes, there is. It's next to the entrance.

B: Thank you for your help!

A: You're welcome. Enjoy your visit!

Writing practice

Read the task, plan your ideas, and write your text in the box. The counter shows how many words you have — it turns green when you're in the right range. Use the grammar from these units. When you finish, compare your text with the example.

Task 1: Questions for a new classmate

Questions and answers50–80 words

You want to know your new classmate better. Write six questions. Then write your own answers.

Write about

  • two questions with be (Are you…? Is your…?)
  • two questions with do / does (Do you…? Does your…?)
  • two open questions (Where…? What…? When…?)
  • your answers (use short answers and add one detail)

Try to use

  • Are you…? / Is your…?
  • Do you…? / Does your…?
  • Where / What / When / Who + question
  • short answers (Yes, I do. No, it isn't.)
0 words
Show example text (64 words)
1. Are you from this city? — No, I'm not. I'm from Lima. 2. Is your family big? — Yes, it is. I have four brothers. 3. Do you work? — Yes, I do. I work in a bank. 4. Does your best friend speak English? — No, she doesn't. 5. Where do you live? — I live near the park. 6. What is your favorite food? — It's pizza!

Task 2: Very different people

Paragraph60–80 words

Write about you and a person in your family or a friend. Say how you are different.

Write about

  • what you are and aren't like
  • what you do and don't do
  • what the other person does and doesn't do
  • one thing you both like or don't like

Try to use

  • I'm not / he isn't / we aren't
  • I don't / she doesn't + base verb
  • but
0 words
Show example text (74 words)
My sister Ana and I are very different. I'm not a morning person, but she is. She gets up at six every day. I don't get up before nine on weekends! Ana doesn't eat meat, but I love burgers. I'm not very organized, and my room isn't tidy. Her room is always clean. She doesn't watch TV, but I watch it every night. But we both love music, and we don't like cold weather.
